skill.name: get-available-resources
skill.description: Detect local CPU, GPU, memory, disk, and operating system resources for scientific computing. The skill writes a resource summary file and recommends parallel, memory, GPU, and large data strategies.
skill.summary: Detect compute resources and choose practical scientific computing strategies.
skill.author: K-Dense-AI

security_audit.summary: The static command-execution alerts are largely false positives: the subprocess calls use fixed argument lists for local hardware utilities, and Markdown backticks are documentation syntax. The main confirmed risk is filesystem impact because the custom output path can overwrite writable files. No evidence of network exfiltration, credential access, obfuscation, or prompt injection was found.

remediation.issue: Custom output path can overwrite files
remediation.suggestion: Restrict --output to the current workspace, refuse existing non-resource files, or require explicit confirmation before overwriting any file.

remediation.issue: Resource inventory is written to a project file
remediation.suggestion: Add .claude_resources.json to generated .gitignore guidance and warn users before sharing files that contain local system details.

remediation.issue: External hardware utilities run during detection
remediation.suggestion: Document the exact local commands and run detection only after the user requests a resource check or approves automatic detection.

content.user_title: Detect Compute Resources for Scientific Work
content.value_statement: Scientific workloads need clear hardware limits before users choose a processing strategy. This skill detects local resources and recommends CPU, memory, GPU, and large data approaches.
actual_capabilities: Detects CPU core counts, architecture, processor details, and optional frequency information.
Measures total and available RAM, swap space, and current memory usage.
Checks disk capacity and available space for the current working directory.
Detects NVIDIA, AMD, and Apple Silicon GPU backends when local utilities are available.
Writes a local resource summary file with strategy recommendations for scientific computing.
Suggests worker counts, memory strategies, GPU libraries, and large data handling approaches.
limitations: GPU detection depends on local utilities such as nvidia-smi, rocm-smi, sysctl, or system_profiler.
Memory and disk results are snapshots and can change during long workflows.
The recommendations are threshold based and do not benchmark real workload performance.
The output file may contain local system details that should not be shared blindly.

use_cases.title: Plan Large Dataset Analysis
use_cases.description: Check memory and disk limits before choosing pandas, Dask, Zarr, HDF5, or streaming workflows.

use_cases.title: Choose Model Training Hardware
use_cases.description: Detect CUDA, ROCm, Metal, or CPU-only environments before selecting machine learning libraries.

use_cases.title: Set Parallel Worker Counts
use_cases.description: Use CPU core data to choose practical worker counts for batch jobs, simulations, and grid searches.

prompt_templates.title: Check Basic Resources
prompt_templates.prompt: Use get-available-resources to summarize my CPU, memory, disk, and GPU availability before this analysis.

prompt_templates.title: Plan Dataset Loading
prompt_templates.prompt: Run get-available-resources, then recommend whether this dataset should use in-memory loading, chunking, or streaming.

prompt_templates.title: Select GPU Backend
prompt_templates.prompt: Use get-available-resources to detect available GPU backends and recommend a training device and library stack.

prompt_templates.title: Tune Parallel Execution
prompt_templates.prompt: Use get-available-resources to design a parallel execution plan with worker counts, memory safeguards, and disk constraints.

output_examples.input: I need to process a 40 GB dataset on this machine.
output: The machine has enough disk space, but available memory is below the dataset size.
Use chunked processing with Dask or Zarr instead of loading the full dataset.
Limit parallel workers so each worker has enough memory for its chunk.

output_examples.input: Can I train this neural network with GPU acceleration?
output: The resource check found a supported GPU backend.
Use the matching framework backend and keep a CPU fallback for portability.
Monitor memory use because available GPU memory can change during training.

output_examples.input: How many workers should I use for this simulation?
output: Use fewer workers than the total logical core count to keep the system responsive.
Start with the suggested worker count, then reduce it if memory use grows quickly.
Re-run the check before scaling the simulation to a larger parameter grid.

best_practices: Run the resource check before major compute decisions, not after a workload fails.
Re-run detection when machine load, available memory, or working directory storage changes.
Treat the resource file as local environment data and avoid committing it by default.
anti_patterns: Assuming a single resource snapshot remains accurate during a long-running workflow.
Using maximum worker counts without considering memory pressure from each worker.
Sharing the generated resource file without reviewing local system details first.

faq.question: What resources does this skill detect?
faq.answer: It detects CPU, memory, disk, operating system, Python version, and supported GPU backends when local tools are available.

faq.question: Does it send my resource data anywhere?
faq.answer: No network behavior was found. The script writes resource data to a local JSON file.

faq.question: Which GPU platforms are supported?
faq.answer: It checks NVIDIA CUDA, AMD ROCm, and Apple Silicon Metal using local platform utilities.

faq.question: Can I choose the output file location?
faq.answer: Yes. The script supports a custom output path, but users should avoid overwriting important files.

faq.question: Are the recommendations exact performance predictions?
faq.answer: No. They are practical starting points based on resource thresholds, not workload benchmarks.

faq.question: When should I run it again?
faq.answer: Run it again before major compute tasks or when memory, disk space, or available hardware may have changed.
